mcqs.question: What separates a strong answer to "name a pattern you've used in a real framework" from a weak one?
options: Explaining the mechanism in your own words with a specific, real method or class, rather than just naming the framework and the pattern
Naming as many frameworks as possible in the time available
Reciting the framework's own official documentation description verbatim
Choosing the most obscure framework possible to sound more experienced
mcqs.explanation: The bar is explaining how the mechanism actually works, grounded in something concrete you could point to in code — not just naming a framework and pattern, reciting documentation, or picking an obscure example for its own sake.

mcqs.question: For OkHttp's Interceptor chain, what's a concrete answer to "why did the framework authors choose Chain of Responsibility over the alternative"?
options: It's simply the newest pattern available, so newer frameworks default to it
It lets each cross-cutting concern live in its own class, and lets consumers add their own interceptors without modifying OkHttp's own source code
It was chosen purely to reduce the total number of classes in the library
It removes the need for OkHttp to support any configuration at all
mcqs.explanation: The real payoff is extensibility without modification: separate concerns into separate interceptor classes, and let external code add to the chain without touching the library's internals. There's no 'newest pattern' rule, the pattern actually adds classes rather than reducing them, and it doesn't remove configuration — Builder still handles that.

mcqs.question: What's a reliable structural tell for spotting the Builder pattern in an unfamiliar codebase, without relying on class names?
options: Any class with more than three fields is a Builder
Any class implementing an interface with a single method
A class with chained methods that each return `this`, ending in a final method like `build()` that produces the finished object
Any class marked final in its declaration
mcqs.explanation: The structural signature — fluent chained calls returning the same instance, capped by a build()-style finishing method — is what actually identifies Builder, independent of naming. Field count, a single-method interface, and the final keyword aren't reliable indicators of this pattern.

mcqs.question: A class is named `ConnectionFactory` but its only method is `new Connection(host, port)` with no branching or type selection. Is this an example of the Factory pattern?
options: Yes, because any class with 'Factory' in its name is using the Factory pattern by definition
Yes, because it constructs an object, which is all the Factory pattern requires
It depends only on whether the method is marked static
No — the name alone isn't evidence; Factory requires hiding a choice among multiple concrete types, which isn't happening here
mcqs.explanation: A class name is a hint to investigate, not proof of a pattern — this method has no polymorphic choice to hide, just a single direct construction, so it isn't Factory in any meaningful sense regardless of its name. Static-ness has no bearing on whether this qualifies.
